asset_name: 「我在场」第一人称历史沉浸结构（瞬间落地-真实性立约-禁入潜入-倒计时撞击-见证崩解）
topic: You're in Pompeii — and the Mountain Has Been Warning You for Days

audience.target_audience: 18-45 悬疑爱好者、美国为主、性别偏男

materials:
一、30秒速览（全部是铁证级事实）
- 公元79年，意大利维苏威火山喷发，掩埋了庞贝、赫库兰尼姆、奥普隆提斯、斯塔比亚等罗马城镇。喷发类型因此被命名为"普林尼式喷发"（Plinian eruption），得名自目击者小普林尼的书信。
- 庞贝全城被埋在约4–6米厚的浮石与火山灰下；赫库兰尼姆被埋在约20多米的火山碎屑堆积下。
- 两城已出土人类遗骸合计超过1500具；总死亡人数至今无法确证。
- 城市在地下保存了约1700年，1748年起系统发掘，1997年列入联合国教科文组织世界遗产名录。
- 唯一可确认姓名的遇难者是罗马舰队司令老普林尼（Pliny the Elder）。
二、唯一的目击者记录：小普林尼的两封书信（文案最核心的素材库）
文献背景【古代文献】：小普林尼（Pliny the Younger，时年17岁）在那不勒斯湾西岸的米塞努姆（Misenum，距火山约30公里）目睹喷发。约25–27年后（约公元106–107年），他应历史学家塔西佗（Tacitus）之请写下两封信（《书信集》第六卷第16封和第20封），成为人类历史上第一份火山喷发的详细目击记录。
可直接引用的书信细节（均出自两封信原文）【古代文献】：
1. 喷发云：他母亲首先注意到一朵"形状和大小都不寻常的云"。小普林尼写道，它"最像一株伞松"——一根极高的"树干"顶端分出若干"枝杈"，时而发白、时而因夹杂尘土而斑驳。
2. 出海救援：其舅父老普林尼（米塞努姆舰队司令）先是出于科学好奇乘船靠近观察；收到火山脚下友人雷克蒂娜（Rectina）的求救信后，改为组织舰队救援。舵手劝他返航时，他说了那句名言："幸运眷顾勇敢者"（拉丁原文：fortes fortuna iuvat）。
3. 夜间避难：老普林尼在斯塔比亚（Stabiae）与朋友过夜，火山多处火光在夜色中清晰可见；房屋被持续地震摇得仿佛脱离地基，众人把枕头绑在头上抵挡落石。
4. 老普林尼之死：次日海边风力未减，老普林尼因烟尘窒息倒下（信中暗示与其脆弱的呼吸系统有关）。两日后遗体被找到，"衣着完好，更像睡着而非死去"。——注意：其具体死因（中风、哮喘发作等）属后世推测【争议/存疑】；另有苏维托尼乌斯记载的"命奴隶了结自己"一说，仅见于该单一来源【争议/存疑】。
5. 白昼如夜：小普林尼自述米塞努姆陷入"比任何黑夜更黑"的黑暗，"像一间密闭的房间"；灰烬如雪，需不断抖落以免被埋；海水后退、海滩上露出搁浅的海洋生物（海水异常后退有书信原文为证，可理解为海啸前兆）。
6. 前兆地震：喷发前多日当地已有频繁震颤，但"坎帕尼亚地区地震司空见惯"，无人警觉。
三、喷发全程：两天时间线（文献记录 + 地层科学重建）
以下时刻以地层学研究重建为主，与小普林尼的记录互相印证【科学研究（重建）】。日期先按传统口径"8月24–25日"表述，日期争议见第七部分。
前兆
- 喷发前数日：持续小规模地震【古代文献：小普林尼书信】。
- 更早的背景：公元62年2月5日大地震曾重创庞贝（详见第四部分），17年后许多建筑仍在修复中【考古实物：全城多处未完工的脚手架和修复痕迹】。
第一天（约下午1时喷发开始）
- 约13:00：巨大喷发柱升起，高约33公里，直入平流层【科学研究；小普林尼记录"第七时左右"出现怪云，两相吻合】。
- 此后约18小时为浮石降落阶段：浮石与火山灰以每小时约15–20厘米的速度堆积，最终在庞贝积到约2.8–3米厚【科学研究】。前期落白色浮石，后期转灰色浮石（对应岩浆成分变化，地层中有明确分界）。
- 这一阶段大多数居民有足够时间逃离城市——这是"多数庞贝人其实活了下来"的依据【科学研究：地层中遇难者分布】。
- 屋顶在浮石重压下陆续坍塌，压死留在室内者。
第二天（火山碎屑流阶段）
- 喷发柱开始周期性崩塌，产生至少6股火山碎屑涌流（编号S1–S6）【科学研究】。
- 前几股吞没了距火山口更近的赫库兰尼姆（约500–600°C）。
- 第4股涌流（S4）是第一股抵达庞贝的涌流，温度约250–300°C。它在庞贝留下的沉积层只有约3厘米厚，却造成庞贝绝大多数遇难者死亡，波及约80平方公里【科学研究：2010年骨骼受热实验比对研究】。
- 喷发总时长约25–32小时（各研究口径略有差异）。
喷发规模关键数字
- 火山爆发指数：VEI 5级【科学研究】
- 喷发柱高度：约33公里【科学研究】
- 峰值喷出速率：约每秒150万吨物质【模型估算，媒体常引用】
- 释放热能：常被科普资料表述为"约10万倍广岛原子弹"【模型估算，非实测】
- 喷出物总量：约3–4立方公里【模型估算】
四、喷发前夜的庞贝：两个有据可查的背景事件
公元59年角斗场骚乱【古代文献+考古实物，双重印证】
- 塔西佗《编年史》第14卷第17章记载：公元59年，庞贝人与邻城努凯里亚人（Nuceria）在角斗表演中从对骂升级为械斗，努凯里亚人伤亡惨重，告到罗马。
- 处罚：元老院禁止庞贝十年内举办此类集会，非法社团解散，表演组织者、被逐出元老院的李维涅乌斯·列古路斯（Livineius Regulus）遭流放。
- 实物佐证：庞贝"阿克提乌斯·阿尼凯图斯之家"出土的骚乱题材壁画（现存那不勒斯国家考古博物馆，编号112222），以及"狄俄斯库里兄弟之家"门墙上的获胜涂鸦"坎帕尼亚人，随着这场胜利，你们与努凯里亚人一同完蛋了"。
公元62年2月5日大地震【古代文献+考古实物】
- 震级据研究估算为5.2–6.1级，最大烈度IX–X度，庞贝与赫库兰尼姆均遭重创。
- 塞内卡（Seneca）在《自然问题》第六卷专章记述此次地震，并记载约600只羊因"毒气"死亡。
- 年代存小争议：塞内卡的执政官纪年指向63年，塔西佗指向62年；意大利强震目录采信62年【争议/存疑：仅年份差一年，事件本身无争议】。
- 实物佐证：庞贝"银行家卢基乌斯·卡埃基利乌斯·尤昆杜斯之家"出土的浮雕，刻画了朱庇特神庙等在地震中受损的场景。
- 关键事实：79年喷发时，全城仍处在震后修复状态（多处工地、未完工的柱廊、正在重修的伊西斯神庙等），庞贝不是一座"完工的样板城"，而是一座"正在施工的城"。
五、遇难者：人数、遗骸与死因研究
遗骸统计（截至2003年权威统计）【考古实物+科学研究】
- 庞贝：出土遗骸1150具（1044具可辨认完整个体 + 约100具零散骨骼推算）。
  - 其中394具（38%）死于浮石降落阶段，90%死于室内——主要因屋顶被浮石压塌。
  - 650具（62%）死于火山碎屑涌流阶段，室内外比例约各半（49%在街道、51%在屋内）。
  - 研究估算未发掘区域内可能仍埋有约464具遗体。
- 赫库兰尼姆：出土遗骸约332具，其中约300具是1980年起在海边船库（拱形石室）内集中发现的——他们挤在船库里等待从海上逃生，密度高达每平方米3人，全部被第一股涌流瞬间杀死。
- 两城合计出土遗骸超过1500具。
- 奥普隆提斯：数十具（姿势研究统计了37具）。
- 总死亡人数无法确证。庞贝人口学界估算约1.1万–1.5万人【模型估算】，推算死亡约2000人。网络上流传的"死亡1.6万人"说法缺乏文献与考古依据【争议/存疑，不建议使用】。
死因研究（重要，可纠正流行误解）【科学研究】
- 2010年（《科学公共图书馆》PLoS ONE，马斯特罗洛伦佐团队）：将出土骨骼与现代实验加热骨骼比对，结合遗骸在地层中的位置，得出结论——主要死因是高温热冲击，而非此前认为的火山灰窒息。S4涌流250–300°C的热浪可在一秒内致死，即使躲在室内也无法幸免。
- 遇难者"定格在动作中"的扭曲姿势，不是长期痛苦挣扎的结果，而是高温引发的尸体痉挛（cadaveric spasm）——这一点是纠正影视夸张描写的硬证据。
- 玻璃化大脑（2020年初报，2025年2月《科学报告》Scientific Reports 确证）：赫库兰尼姆"奥古斯都祭司学院"一具20世纪60年代出土、俯卧于床上的男性遗骸，其颅骨内发现深色有机玻璃状物质。分析表明脑组织曾被加热到至少510°C再急速冷却——这是考古遗址中已知唯一的有机物玻璃案例，也证明杀死赫库兰尼姆人的首个致命事件是极热而短暂的火山灰云，而非后来掩埋城市的碎屑流（后者温度不超过465°C）。
唯一可确认姓名的遇难者
- 老普林尼：有外甥小普林尼的书信直接记录【古代文献】。
- 赫罗底家族的德鲁西拉（Drusilla）及其子阿格里帕：仅见于约瑟夫斯《犹太古史》提及【争议/存疑：单一来源】。
六、被埋前的庞贝：城市数据档案【考古实物】
- 建城：由奥斯坎人（Osci）建于公元前7–6世纪；最早的"pappamonte"火山灰岩城墙圈围约63.5公顷。历经希腊、萨莫奈文化影响；公元前89年被苏拉（Sulla）军队围攻，公元前80年成为罗马殖民地，正式名称"科尔内利亚·维内里亚·庞佩亚诺鲁姆"（Colonia Cornelia Veneria Pompeianorum）。
- 规模：全城约66公顷，已发掘约44公顷（约三分之二），出土约1500座建筑。人口学界估算约1.1万–1.5万【模型估算】。
- 圆形竞技场：约建于公元前70年，是现存最古老的罗马石砌竞技场，比罗马斗兽场早一个多世纪，可容纳约2万人。
- 市井生活硬数据：至少33家面包房（多数自带磨坊）、80多家"热食铺"（thermopolium，古罗马快餐柜台）、全城记录在案的涂鸦铭文超过1.1万条（竞选标语、情诗、角斗士八卦、账单，应有尽有）。
- 地标建筑：广场（Forum，38×142米）；巴西利卡大会堂（或为现存最古老的巴西利卡）；农牧神之家（出土著名的《亚历山大马赛克》）；神秘别墅（约90个房间，酒神狄俄尼索斯秘仪壁画长17米、绘29个人物）；已确认的妓院（Lupanar，石床与门上情色壁画为实物证据）。
- 供水：铅管供水系统、公共喷泉、公共浴室带地暖（hypocaust）——均有实物。
七、喷发日期之争：8月24日还是10月24日？（文案必须写对的一段）
传统口径：公元79年8月24日
- 依据一：小普林尼书信的手抄本记为"9月朔日前第9日"（nonum kal. Septembres），即8月24日【古代文献——但注意：原稿已佚，现存均为中世纪抄本，各抄本日期从8月到11月不一】。
- 依据二：卡西乌斯·狄奥《罗马史》（约2–3世纪写成）记为"夏末"，与8月说吻合【古代文献】。
10月下旬说的物证
- 遇难者衣着较厚、现场有取暖火盆、秋季果实（栗子、无花果、石榴）、已封罐发酵的新葡萄酒（葡萄通常9月下旬才收）；2007年风向研究认为火山碎屑分布与秋季主导风向吻合【考古实物+科学研究，均属间接推断】。
- 2018年关键发现：第五区一座正在装修的房屋墙上发现炭笔涂鸦"XVI K NOV"（"11月朔日前第16日"，即10月17日）。炭笔极易被抹掉，发掘方据此认为写于喷发前数日，喷发应在10月24日前后【考古实物】。
反方证据（支持8月说）
- 炭笔耐久性实验表明，炭笔涂鸦在庞贝环境下可以从10月保存到次年8月，不足以推翻8月说【科学研究】。
- 曾被引为"10月铁证"的"金手镯之家"提图斯皇帝铜币（原释读为第15次统帅头衔 IMP XV，即79年9月8日之后铸造），经大英博物馆钱币学家理查德·阿布迪（Richard Abdy）重新释读为 IMP XIII——磨损严重的旧释读有误，该币不再构成8月说的障碍【科学研究】。
- 2024年《科学进展》（Science Advances）发表氩-氩测年研究（1938±10年），作者系统梳理文献证据后结论：现有最佳证据支持8月24日【科学研究】。
文案建议口径："喷发日期传统上记为8月24日，2018年炭笔铭文等物证曾引发'10月24日'之争，2024年最新测年与文献综合研究重新支持8月24日——但需注意，两种日期都仍有学者讨论。"绝不能只写其中一个日期并当成铁案。
八、灾后：罗马官方的反应【古代文献】
- 皇帝提图斯（Titus，79年6月即位）任命两名前执政官级别的专员主持坎帕尼亚救济，并将遇难且无继承人者的财产用于灾区重建（苏维托尼乌斯《提图斯传》第8章；卡西乌斯·狄奥《罗马史》66卷亦有记载）。
- 幸存者与盗掘者很快回到废墟挖掘财物——现代考古发现房屋墙上留有"此屋已挖"的古罗马涂鸦，以及盗掘地道痕迹【考古实物：证明庞贝并非"被遗忘后完整封存"，这是常被忽略的冷知识】。
- 此后约1600年间，城市的名称与位置逐渐失传。
九、重见天日：发掘史时间线【考古实物+档案】
- 1592年：建筑师多梅尼科·丰塔纳（Domenico Fontana）开凿引水渠时挖到带壁画的古墙与铭文，未受重视，重新掩埋。
- 1689–1699年：挖井发现提及"庞贝市政官"的铭文；朱塞佩·马克里尼在1699年《论维苏威》中提出古城埋在"拉奇维塔"（La Civita）之下。
- 1738年：那不勒斯国王查理三世（波旁家族）为建夏宫打地基时发现赫库兰尼姆，开始地下坑道式盗掘。
- 1748年：西班牙军事工程师罗克·华金·德·阿尔库比埃雷（Rocque Joaquin de Alcubierre）主持启动庞贝发掘（早期实为寻宝式挖掘，大量文物无记录流入王室收藏）；同年4月19日出土第一具人骨。
- 1763年8月20日：出土铭文"……Rei Publicae Pompeianorum……"（庞贝公共事务），城市身份正式确认。
- 1764年起：卡尔·韦伯（Karl Weber）主导首次科学化发掘；法国统治时期（1806–1815）一度动用700名工人。
- 1863–1875年：朱塞佩·菲奥雷利（Giuseppe Fiorelli）主持发掘，两大创举沿用至今——①石膏铸模法：向尸体腐烂后在火山灰中留下的空腔灌注石膏，重现遇难者最后一刻的姿态（今天改用更耐久的透明树脂，且不损伤骨骼）；②将全城划分为9个"区"（regiones）和若干"街区"（insulae）并给每座房屋编号的定位系统。他1873–74年修建的庞贝文物馆（Antiquarium）至今仍在使用。
- 1882年：奥古斯特·毛（Auguste Mau）创立庞贝壁画"四种风格"分类体系，沿用至今。
- 1924–1961年：阿梅代奥·马伊里（Amedeo Maiuri）主持大规模发掘，50年代基本挖完阿邦丹扎大道以南区域（但记录质量差，至今困扰研究者）。
- 1943年：二战盟军轰炸损毁多座建筑（包括文物馆）。
- 1980年：伊尔皮尼亚大地震再次重创遗址。
- 1997年：庞贝、赫库兰尼姆、托雷安农齐亚塔（奥普隆提斯）整体列入联合国教科文组织世界遗产名录（编号829）。
- 2010年:"角斗士学校"（Schola Armaturarum）因暴雨坍塌，引发全球对遗址保护不力的批评。
- 2012年起：欧盟资助的"大庞贝项目"（Grande Progetto Pompei）启动，重心从发掘转向保护，加固了超过2.5公里危墙。
- 2024年起：遗址限流，每日最多发售2万张实名制门票（年访客量约250–400万）。
十、近年重大新发现（2018–2025，都是很好的文案素材）【考古实物】
- 2018年12月：神秘别墅出土一匹仍佩戴全套马具的马匹遗骸。
- 2018年10月：发现"10月17日"炭笔铭文（详见第七部分日期之争）。
- 2020年11月：西维塔·朱利安那（Civita Giuliana）出土两具男性遗骸（2米厚灰层中），骨骼分析显示年轻者长期从事体力劳动（推测为奴隶），两人疑躲过第一天、死于次日涌流。
- 2020年12月：第五区完整发掘一座热食铺，8个陶罐内仍存鸭、山羊、猪、鱼、蜗牛等食物残渣；柜台壁画绘有拴绳狗；出土一具肩高仅20–25厘米的成年小型犬骨架（古罗马选育宠物犬的实证）。
- 2021年1月：西维塔·朱利安那别墅门廊出土一辆保存完好的四轮礼仪式马车（青铜与红黑木饰板），后确认为古罗马婚车"pilentum"，2023年修复后在罗马戴克里先浴场展出。
- 2021年：萨尔诺门外发现获释奴隶马库斯·韦内利乌斯·塞昆迪奥（Marcus Venerius Secundio）的彩绘墓葬，含部分木乃伊化遗骸；铭文记载他曾任维纳斯神庙管理员并举办过希腊语戏剧演出——庞贝存在希腊文化活动的首个实证。
- 2024年4月：第九区诺拉之路出土一间15×6米的"黑色宴会厅"，墙面绘有特洛伊战争题材罕见壁画（海伦与帕里斯、阿波罗与卡珊德拉）。
- 2024年6月：第九区出土一间罕见的蓝色神龛（约8平方米），绘四季女神，出土15个双耳罐、青铜水壶与油灯。
- 2025年：出土一座大型私家浴场宅邸，发现与真人等大的酒神狄俄尼索斯秘仪主题壁画。
十一、维苏威火山今天（收尾素材）
- 维苏威是欧洲大陆唯一的活火山（复式火山，位于更古老的索马山破火口内），海拔1281米【科学研究】。
- 喷发史：公元79年大喷发后仍有多次活动（472年、1631年等），1631年喷发致数千人死亡；最近一次喷发为1944年3月17–29日——时值二战，美军拍摄了大量影像，火山弹与火山灰摧毁了附近机场约78架美军B-25轰炸机【档案记录】。
- 世界最古老的火山观测站：维苏威火山观测台1841年3月10日由两西西里国王费迪南多二世创立，现由意大利国家地球物理与火山学研究所（INGV）运营，24小时监测地震、地形形变与气体。
- 风险现状：官方划定"红色区域"覆盖那不勒斯与萨莱诺两省25个市镇、约60万人；更广的那不勒斯都市圈约300万人生活在影响范围内。意大利民防预案以"喷发前数日预警、提前撤离红区"为设想，但预案可行性长期受到专家质疑【官方文件+学界评论】。
- 当前警戒级别为绿色（常态级），无迫在眉睫喷发的迹象【INGV公开信息，截至本资料整理日】。
十二、常见讹传与措辞红线（防踩坑）
可以直接说的（铁证）：
- "喷发云像一株伞松"——目击者书信原文
- "幸运眷顾勇敢者"——老普林尼遗言级别的名言，书信原文
- "庞贝被埋4–6米、赫库兰尼姆被埋20多米"
- "遇难者主要死于高温热冲击而非窒息"——2010年同行评审研究
- "角斗场骚乱、十年禁赛"——塔西佗记载+壁画实物双重印证
- "石膏铸模重现遇难者姿态，1863年菲奥雷利发明"
必须加限定词的：
- 喷发日期 → 按第七部分口径写，两个日期都要提
- "约1.1万人口、约2000死亡" → 加"据学界估算"
- "每秒150万吨、10万倍广岛原子弹" → 加"据模型估算"
- 老普林尼具体死因 → "书信未明言，后世有窒息/中风等推测"
- "玻璃化大脑" → 可写，注明2025年《科学报告》研究
绝不能说的：
- "全城人在睡梦中瞬间团灭"（错：浮石阶段持续约18小时，多数人已逃离）
- "岩浆吞没了庞贝"（错：掩埋城市的是浮石、火山灰与火山碎屑流，没有岩浆流进这两座城）
- "死亡1.6万人"（网络流传数字，无依据）
- "喷发日期是铁定的8月24日/10月24日"（争议未完全平息，2024年研究支持8月24日）
- "庞贝被完整封存、无人知晓直到1748年"（错：灾后即有盗掘，1592年已有接触）

thesis_card.viewer_belief: 庞贝人被火山'瞬间'吞没，毫无预警地死在睡梦中
thesis_card.truth: 喷发持续32小时，前17小时浮石降落阶段多数人有时间逃离；但频繁地震已是常态（62年大地震后17年仍在修复），无人将震颤与火山联系；喷发过程中仍有地震导致墙体坍塌砸死幸存者；次日火山碎屑涌流以高温在瞬间杀死留守者（死因学界仍有窒息vs热冲击争议）；多数庞贝人活了下来，但1150具遗骸的姿态与最新发掘证明：留下的人经历了从'日常'到'炼狱'的极速坠落
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 庞贝不是瞬间消失的——它用17小时给了人们逃生窗口，却因'地震是常态'的麻木让许多人留守，最终被次日的热浪或坍塌在瞬间杀死；'读过'与'活过'是两回事，当危险成为日常的一部分，你就不再把它当成危险——直到倒计时归零
thesis_card.ending_landing: 结尾落在'当危险成为日常的一部分，你就不再把它当成危险——直到倒计时归零'的主题对照句，用小普林尼的'比任何黑夜更黑'意象收束，补充'2023年发现的两具遗骸：他们躲过了第一天，却死于地震'的最新证据强化'多重杀伤'主题，无CTA
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 原片结论'读过与活过是两回事'的情感内核保留，但庞贝题材增加了两层深化：①'麻木'机制——泰坦尼克号的人不知道会撞冰山，庞贝人则是'知道火山在那儿、知道会地震，但17年来一直没事'；②'多重杀伤'机制——不是单一灾难，而是浮石、地震、碎屑流的复合致死，2023-2025年新发掘持续揭示更多死亡方式

facts.content: 公元79年约下午1时（小普林尼书信记'第七时'），意大利维苏威火山喷发，喷发柱高约33公里
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第16封；火山学重建研究

facts.content: 喷发总时长约25-32小时，分两阶段：前18小时浮石降落（庞贝堆积2.8-3米厚），次日火山碎屑涌流阶段（至少6股，编号S1-S6）
facts.source: 地层学与火山学重建研究

facts.content: 庞贝被埋在约4-6米厚的浮石与火山灰下，赫库兰尼姆被埋在约20多米的火山碎屑堆积下
facts.source: 考古发掘记录

facts.content: 庞贝出土遗骸约1150具，赫库兰尼姆约332具（其中约300具集中在船库），两城合计超过1500具；另有研究提及周边区域合计超过2300具
facts.source: 2003年庞贝统计（R2, R3）；1980年代赫库兰尼姆船库发掘；巴西媒体综合报道

facts.content: 庞贝遗骸中约38%死于浮石降落阶段（多因屋顶坍塌），约62%死于火山碎屑涌流阶段；2023年新发现两具遗骸死于地震导致的墙体坍塌
facts.source: 遇难者分布研究（原资料）；2023年《地球科学前沿》地震研究

facts.content: 2023年X射线分析研究支持窒息为主要死因（victims choked on ash）；但2010年骨骼受热实验研究曾提出高温热冲击说（S4涌流250-300°C可在瞬间致死）；学界对死因仍有争议
facts.source: 2023年《科学公共图书馆》PLoS ONE研究；2010年马斯特罗洛伦佐团队研究

facts.content: 庞贝人口估算约1.1万-1.5万人（也有估算3万人），赫库兰尼姆约5000人；推算死亡约2000人或更多（一说可达1.5万）；多数居民在浮石降落阶段逃离
facts.source: 人口学模型估算；德国考古学家综述
facts.method: 城市面积66公顷 × 古罗马城市人口密度估算 → 1.1万-3万人口；出土遗骸1150具 + 周边区域推算 → 死亡约2000-1.5万；逃生率根据人口上限不同在50%-90%之间

facts.content: 庞贝全城约66公顷，已发掘约44公顷，出土约1500座建筑，包括圆形竞技场（可容纳2万人）、广场（38×142米）、神秘别墅（约90个房间）、农牧神之家等
facts.source: 考古发掘记录

facts.content: 至少33家面包房（多数自带磨坊）、80多家热食铺（thermopolium）、全城记录在案的涂鸦铭文超过1.1万条
facts.source: 考古发掘记录与铭文统计

facts.content: 公元62年2月5日大地震（估算5.2-6.1级）重创庞贝，79年喷发时全城仍在修复状态（多处脚手架、未完工的伊西斯神庙）；喷发前数日持续小规模震颤
facts.source: 塔西佗《编年史》；塞内卡《自然问题》第六卷；考古实物

facts.content: 小普林尼书信记载：'坎帕尼亚地区地震司空见惯'，无人将喷发前的震颤视为异常
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第20封

facts.content: 1863年朱塞佩·菲奥雷利发明石膏铸模法：向尸体腐烂后在火山灰中留下的空腔灌注石膏，重现遇难者最后姿态
facts.source: 考古技术史记录

facts.slot: 唯一确认姓名的遇难者
facts.content: 唯一可确认姓名的遇难者是罗马舰队司令老普林尼（Pliny the Elder），因烟尘窒息倒下，遗体两日后被找到'衣着完好，更像睡着而非死去'
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第16封

facts.content: 小普林尼描述喷发云'最像一株伞松'——一根极高的'树干'顶端分出若干'枝杈'，时而发白、时而因夹杂尘土而斑驳
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第16封
facts.region: 意大利米塞努姆（距火山约30公里）

facts.content: 小普林尼自述米塞努姆（距火山30公里）陷入'比任何黑夜更黑'的黑暗，'像一间密闭的房间'；灰烬如雪，需不断抖落以免被埋
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第20封

facts.slot: 赫库兰尼姆船库遇难者
facts.content: 1980年起在赫库兰尼姆海边船库（拱形石室）内集中发现约300具遗骸，密度高达每平方米3人，全部被第一股涌流瞬间杀死
facts.source: 1980s考古发掘记录

facts.content: 公元59年，庞贝人与邻城努凯里亚人在角斗表演中从对骂升级为械斗，努凯里亚人伤亡惨重；元老院禁止庞贝十年内举办此类集会
facts.source: 塔西佗《编年史》第14卷第17章；庞贝壁画实物（那不勒斯国家考古博物馆编号112222）

facts.content: 2020年12月第五区完整发掘一座热食铺，8个陶罐内仍存鸭、山羊、猪、鱼、蜗牛等食物残渣；柜台壁画绘有拴绳狗
facts.source: 2020年考古发掘新闻稿

facts.content: 传统记为8月24日（小普林尼书信手抄本记'9月朔日前第9日'），2018年炭笔铭文'10月17日'引发争议，2024年《科学进展》综合研究仍支持8月24日
facts.source: 2024年《科学进展》（Science Advances）氩-氩测年研究

facts.content: 2021年在Civita Giuliana发现奴隶房间，面积约16平方米，三张木制床（两张约1.7米、一张约1.4米，可调节长度），床由粗板和绳网搭成；房间无装饰，仅高处有小窗，床下有便壶和陶罐；角落有8个双耳瓶和装有马具的木箱
facts.source: 2021年庞贝考古公园发掘报告

facts.content: 唯一可确认姓名的遇难者是老普林尼（舰队司令）；2021年发现获释奴隶马库斯·韦内利乌斯·塞昆迪奥墓葬（但他是墓葬而非遇难现场）；普通居民的涂鸦超过1.1万条，多为竞选标语、广告和个人留言，但未记录遇难者具体姓名
facts.source: 考古铭文记录；涂鸦研究（Tanzer 1939等）

facts.content: 2025年《地质学会杂志》研究将喷发时长从19小时延长至32小时，识别出17次火山碎屑流；喷发约在中午12时开始（比传统认为的下午1时提前1小时）；浮石降落持续约17小时；火山碎屑流阶段从次日凌晨开始，S4涌流具体抵达庞贝时刻仍为'次日上午'，未见精确到分钟的时间戳
facts.source: 2025年《地质学会杂志》Claudio Scarpati团队研究

facts.slot: 城市空间与社会阶层分布
facts.content: 庞贝存在不同社会阶层聚居的街区（neighborhoods/vici），但无证据显示贵族区与平民区之间有物理隔离（城墙或警卫）；阶层差异体现在住宅规模、装饰和街道位置；工人阶级街区如VIII.7区靠近Porta Stabiana城门，主要街道via Stabbana沿线；贵族别墅多位于城市北部和西部安静区域
facts.source: 庞贝城市结构研究（Ellis & Devore 2005-2006, Gorham 2018）

facts.content: 2020年热食铺发掘发现鸭、山羊、猪、鱼、蜗牛等食物残渣保存在陶罐中；根据罗马帝国同期平民饮食记录，三等舱式底层居民典型食物包括豆汤、鱼、面包、橄榄油、葡萄酒；具体到79年8月24日庞贝某一餐的菜单无考古记录
facts.source: 2020年热食铺发掘；罗马帝国饮食史研究

facts.slot: 喷发前地震活动与幸存者返回
facts.content: 2023年5月发现的两具男性遗骸（位于浮石层之上）证明他们从喷发第一阶段幸存，但死于火山碎屑流到来前的地震导致墙体坍塌；2025年研究发现喷发后有幸存者和外来者返回废墟居住，留下'此屋已挖'的涂鸦和盗掘地道
facts.source: 2024年《地球科学前沿》；2025年庞贝Insula Meridionalis发掘

facts.slot: 赫库兰尼姆玻璃化大脑
facts.content: 2025年2月《科学报告》确证：赫库兰尼姆'奥古斯都祭司学院'一具男性遗骸颅骨内发现玻璃化脑组织，脑组织曾被加热至至少510°C再急速冷却；这是考古遗址中已知唯一的有机物玻璃化案例
facts.source: 2025年《科学报告》Scientific Reports

thesis_check.note: 反转结论'多数庞贝人活了下来，但留下的人因麻木和多重灾难而死'由以下事实撑住：F02+F22（前17-18小时浮石降落给了逃生窗口，总时长32小时）+ F05（62%遇难者死于涌流阶段，2023年新发现地震也致死）+ F06（死因有窒息和热冲击两说，学界仍争议）+ F07（逃生率50-90%，取决于人口估算）+ F10（62年大地震后全城仍在修复）+ F11（'地震司空见惯'的麻木心态）+ F25（2023年发现两具遗骸躲过第一阶段却死于地震）。无相反事实。死因争议已在F06反映，不构成矛盾。

title.fix: 标题方向与框架核心动作（第一人称在场、倒计时见证）完全一致，无需调整

thesis_card.viewer_belief: 庞贝人被火山'瞬间'吞没，毫无预警地死在睡梦中
thesis_card.truth: 喷发持续约25小时，前18小时浮石降落阶段多数人有时间逃离；但频繁地震已是常态（62年大地震后），无人将震颤与火山联系；次日火山碎屑涌流（S4）以250-300°C高温在一秒内杀死留守者——不是窒息，是热冲击；多数庞贝人活了下来，但1150具遗骸的姿态证明：留下的人经历了从'日常'到'炼狱'的极速坠落
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 庞贝不是瞬间消失的——它用18小时给了人们逃生窗口，却因'地震是常态'的麻木让多数人留守，最终被次日的热浪在一秒内杀死；'读过'与'活过'是两回事，当震颤变成日常，灾难就成了看不见的倒计时
thesis_card.ending_landing: 结尾落在'当危险成为日常的一部分，你就不再把它当成危险——直到倒计时归零'的主题对照句，用小普林尼的'比任何黑夜更黑'意象收束，无CTA
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 原片结论'读过与活过是两回事'的情感内核保留，但庞贝题材增加了一层'麻木'机制：泰坦尼克号的人不知道会撞冰山，庞贝人则是'知道火山在那儿、知道会地震，但17年来一直没事'——这是一种更深层的悲剧：不是信息缺失，而是日常化导致的警觉失效

adjustments.reason: FS06需要底层居民的真实姓名与身份，用于'同桌对白'场景。现有资料仅确认老普林尼一人姓名，需查证：①是否有铭文或涂鸦记录普通居民姓名；②如无，需在稿中明确标注为'假设的同桌对话'并说明依据（如某区域出土的多具遗骸、职业推测）
FS05日常生活流需要具体的住宅细节：①底层住宅的房间尺寸、床铺材质、气味描述；②公共厕所的位置与使用方式；③街道的铺装材料与宽度。现有资料提及'33家面包房、80家热食铺'但缺乏单个住宅内部的量化细节
原片FS03任务简报设定为'探索头等舱+警告船长'双线。庞贝题材中'警告'任务不成立（主角无法改变历史），需改为'探索贵族区+见证最后的日常'双线：①探索目标改为神秘别墅、农牧神之家等禁区；②干预目标改为'记录下这些人最后的样子'（对应FS12-FS13段的情绪任务）
原片FS12-FS13为'计划警告+警告失败'的干预任务线。庞贝题材无'可警告的决策者'（火山喷发无法阻止），需换内容保功能为'无力旁观的情绪累积'：①FS12改为主角在贵族别墅见证'宴会仍在继续、无人察觉危险'的场景；②FS13改为主角意识到'我什么都做不了'的无力感闭合，对应PK06情绪峰值
FS14倒计时段需要精确到分钟的时间线：①S4涌流抵达庞贝的具体时刻（现有资料仅确认'次日上午'）；②浮石降落结束到涌流抵达的时间间隔；③涌流推进速度。需查证火山学重建研究中是否有更精确的时间戳
FS04登船关卡段需要庞贝城内的'阶层检查点'：①贵族区与平民区之间是否有物理隔离（城门、警卫）；②如无，需改为'社会地位的隐形边界'（如服饰、随从数量）作为潜入障碍
FS11调性切换段需要'明天就是那个日子'的具体日期锚点。现有资料存在8月24日vs10月24日争议，需在稿中处理：①采用2024年最新研究支持的8月24日；②在旁白中简短提及争议（'传统上记为8月24日，近年有学者提出10月说，但最新研究仍支持8月'）

facts.content: 公元79年约下午1时（小普林尼书信记'第七时'），意大利维苏威火山喷发，喷发柱高约33公里
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第16封；火山学重建研究

facts.content: 喷发总时长约25-32小时，分两阶段：前18小时浮石降落（庞贝堆积2.8-3米厚），次日火山碎屑涌流阶段（至少6股，编号S1-S6）
facts.source: 地层学与火山学重建研究

facts.content: 庞贝被埋在约4-6米厚的浮石与火山灰下，赫库兰尼姆被埋在约20多米的火山碎屑堆积下
facts.source: 考古发掘记录

facts.content: 庞贝出土遗骸1150具（1044具完整+约100具零散），赫库兰尼姆约332具，两城合计超过1500具
facts.source: 2003年权威统计（庞贝）；1980s发掘记录（赫库兰尼姆船库）

facts.content: 庞贝1150具遗骸中：38%（394具）死于浮石降落阶段（多因屋顶坍塌），62%（650具）死于火山碎屑涌流阶段
facts.source: 2003年遇难者分布研究

facts.content: 2010年骨骼受热实验研究证实：主要死因是高温热冲击（S4涌流250-300°C），而非窒息；热浪可在一秒内致死
facts.source: 2010年《科学公共图书馆》PLoS ONE，马斯特罗洛伦佐团队

facts.content: 庞贝人口学界估算约1.1万-1.5万人，推算死亡约2000人，意味着多数居民在浮石降落阶段（前18小时）逃离
facts.source: 人口学模型估算
facts.method: 城市面积66公顷 × 古罗马城市平均人口密度 → 估算总人口1.1万-1.5万；出土遗骸1150具 + 未发掘区推算464具 ≈ 1600具 → 外推总死亡约2000人 → 逃生率约85-87%

facts.content: 庞贝全城约66公顷，已发掘约44公顷，出土约1500座建筑，包括圆形竞技场（可容纳2万人）、广场（38×142米）、神秘别墅（约90个房间）、农牧神之家等
facts.source: 考古发掘记录

facts.content: 至少33家面包房（多数自带磨坊）、80多家热食铺（thermopolium）、全城记录在案的涂鸦铭文超过1.1万条
facts.source: 考古发掘记录与铭文统计

facts.content: 公元62年2月5日大地震（估算5.2-6.1级）重创庞贝，79年喷发时全城仍在修复状态（多处脚手架、未完工的伊西斯神庙）；喷发前数日持续小规模震颤
facts.source: 塔西佗《编年史》；塞内卡《自然问题》第六卷；考古实物

facts.content: 小普林尼书信记载：'坎帕尼亚地区地震司空见惯'，无人将喷发前的震颤视为异常
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第20封

facts.content: 1863年朱塞佩·菲奥雷利发明石膏铸模法：向尸体腐烂后在火山灰中留下的空腔灌注石膏，重现遇难者最后姿态
facts.source: 考古技术史记录

facts.slot: 唯一确认姓名的遇难者
facts.content: 唯一可确认姓名的遇难者是罗马舰队司令老普林尼（Pliny the Elder），因烟尘窒息倒下，遗体两日后被找到'衣着完好，更像睡着而非死去'
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第16封

facts.content: 小普林尼描述喷发云'最像一株伞松'——一根极高的'树干'顶端分出若干'枝杈'，时而发白、时而因夹杂尘土而斑驳
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第16封
facts.region: 意大利米塞努姆（距火山约30公里）

facts.content: 小普林尼自述米塞努姆（距火山30公里）陷入'比任何黑夜更黑'的黑暗，'像一间密闭的房间'；灰烬如雪，需不断抖落以免被埋
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第20封

facts.slot: 赫库兰尼姆船库遇难者
facts.content: 1980年起在赫库兰尼姆海边船库（拱形石室）内集中发现约300具遗骸，密度高达每平方米3人，全部被第一股涌流瞬间杀死
facts.source: 1980s考古发掘记录

facts.content: 公元59年，庞贝人与邻城努凯里亚人在角斗表演中从对骂升级为械斗，努凯里亚人伤亡惨重；元老院禁止庞贝十年内举办此类集会
facts.source: 塔西佗《编年史》第14卷第17章；庞贝壁画实物（那不勒斯国家考古博物馆编号112222）

facts.content: 2020年12月第五区完整发掘一座热食铺，8个陶罐内仍存鸭、山羊、猪、鱼、蜗牛等食物残渣；柜台壁画绘有拴绳狗
facts.source: 2020年考古发掘新闻稿

facts.content: 传统记为8月24日（小普林尼书信手抄本记'9月朔日前第9日'），2018年炭笔铭文'10月17日'引发争议，2024年《科学进展》综合研究仍支持8月24日
facts.source: 2024年《科学进展》（Science Advances）氩-氩测年研究

facts.content: 需要具体的底层住宅房间尺寸、床铺材质、气味来源（汗味、煤烟、湿木头的考古依据）

facts.slot: 待查-S4涌流精确抵达时刻
facts.content: S4涌流抵达庞贝的具体时刻（现有资料仅确认'次日上午'），以及浮石降落结束到涌流抵达的时间间隔

title.viewer_question: 庞贝人在火山喷发前有没有察觉到危险？他们为什么不逃？最后一刻到底发生了什么？
title.expected_answer_direction: 观众期待看到'火山喷发前的日常生活'与'灾难降临瞬间'的强烈对比，以及'如果我在场会怎样'的沉浸体验

thesis_card.viewer_belief: 庞贝人被火山'瞬间'吞没，毫无预警地死在睡梦中
thesis_card.truth: 喷发持续约25小时，前18小时浮石降落阶段多数人有时间逃离；但频繁地震已是常态（62年大地震后），无人将震颤与火山联系；次日火山碎屑涌流（S4）以250-300°C高温在一秒内杀死留守者——不是窒息，是热冲击；多数庞贝人活了下来，但1150具遗骸的姿态证明：留下的人经历了从'日常'到'炼狱'的极速坠落
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 庞贝不是瞬间消失的——它用18小时给了人们逃生窗口，却因'地震是常态'的麻木让多数人留守，最终被次日的热浪在一秒内杀死；'读过'与'活过'是两回事，当震颤变成日常，灾难就成了看不见的倒计时
thesis_card.ending_landing: 结尾落在'当危险成为日常的一部分，你就不再把它当成危险——直到倒计时归零'的主题对照句，用小普林尼的'比任何黑夜更黑'意象收束，无CTA
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 原片结论'读过与活过是两回事'的情感内核保留，但庞贝题材增加了一层'麻木'机制：泰坦尼克号的人不知道会撞冰山，庞贝人则是'知道火山在那儿、知道会地震，但17年来一直没事'——这是一种更深层的悲剧：不是信息缺失，而是日常化导致的警觉失效

facts.content: 公元79年约下午1时（小普林尼书信记'第七时'），意大利维苏威火山喷发，喷发柱高约33公里
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第16封；火山学重建研究

facts.content: 喷发总时长约25-32小时，分两阶段：前18小时浮石降落（庞贝堆积2.8-3米厚），次日火山碎屑涌流阶段（至少6股，编号S1-S6）
facts.source: 地层学与火山学重建研究

facts.content: 庞贝被埋在约4-6米厚的浮石与火山灰下，赫库兰尼姆被埋在约20多米的火山碎屑堆积下
facts.source: 考古发掘记录

facts.content: 庞贝出土遗骸1150具（1044具完整+约100具零散），赫库兰尼姆约332具，两城合计超过1500具
facts.source: 2003年权威统计（庞贝）；1980s发掘记录（赫库兰尼姆船库）

facts.content: 庞贝1150具遗骸中：38%（394具）死于浮石降落阶段（多因屋顶坍塌），62%（650具）死于火山碎屑涌流阶段
facts.source: 2003年遇难者分布研究

facts.content: 2010年骨骼受热实验研究证实：主要死因是高温热冲击（S4涌流250-300°C），而非窒息；热浪可在一秒内致死
facts.source: 2010年《科学公共图书馆》PLoS ONE，马斯特罗洛伦佐团队

facts.content: 庞贝人口学界估算约1.1万-1.5万人，推算死亡约2000人，意味着多数居民在浮石降落阶段（前18小时）逃离
facts.source: 人口学模型估算
facts.method: 城市面积66公顷 × 古罗马城市平均人口密度 → 估算总人口1.1万-1.5万；出土遗骸1150具 + 未发掘区推算464具 ≈ 1600具 → 外推总死亡约2000人 → 逃生率约85-87%

facts.content: 庞贝全城约66公顷，已发掘约44公顷，出土约1500座建筑，包括圆形竞技场（可容纳2万人）、广场（38×142米）、神秘别墅（约90个房间）、农牧神之家等
facts.source: 考古发掘记录

facts.content: 至少33家面包房（多数自带磨坊）、80多家热食铺（thermopolium）、全城记录在案的涂鸦铭文超过1.1万条
facts.source: 考古发掘记录与铭文统计

facts.content: 公元62年2月5日大地震（估算5.2-6.1级）重创庞贝，79年喷发时全城仍在修复状态（多处脚手架、未完工的伊西斯神庙）；喷发前数日持续小规模震颤
facts.source: 塔西佗《编年史》；塞内卡《自然问题》第六卷；考古实物

facts.content: 小普林尼书信记载：'坎帕尼亚地区地震司空见惯'，无人将喷发前的震颤视为异常
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第20封

facts.content: 1863年朱塞佩·菲奥雷利发明石膏铸模法：向尸体腐烂后在火山灰中留下的空腔灌注石膏，重现遇难者最后姿态
facts.source: 考古技术史记录

facts.slot: 唯一确认姓名的遇难者
facts.content: 唯一可确认姓名的遇难者是罗马舰队司令老普林尼（Pliny the Elder），因烟尘窒息倒下，遗体两日后被找到'衣着完好，更像睡着而非死去'
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第16封

facts.content: 小普林尼描述喷发云'最像一株伞松'——一根极高的'树干'顶端分出若干'枝杈'，时而发白、时而因夹杂尘土而斑驳
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第16封
facts.region: 意大利米塞努姆（距火山约30公里）

facts.content: 小普林尼自述米塞努姆（距火山30公里）陷入'比任何黑夜更黑'的黑暗，'像一间密闭的房间'；灰烬如雪，需不断抖落以免被埋
facts.source: 小普林尼《书信集》第六卷第20封

facts.slot: 赫库兰尼姆船库遇难者
facts.content: 1980年起在赫库兰尼姆海边船库（拱形石室）内集中发现约300具遗骸，密度高达每平方米3人，全部被第一股涌流瞬间杀死
facts.source: 1980s考古发掘记录

facts.content: 公元59年，庞贝人与邻城努凯里亚人在角斗表演中从对骂升级为械斗，努凯里亚人伤亡惨重；元老院禁止庞贝十年内举办此类集会
facts.source: 塔西佗《编年史》第14卷第17章；庞贝壁画实物（那不勒斯国家考古博物馆编号112222）

facts.content: 2020年12月第五区完整发掘一座热食铺，8个陶罐内仍存鸭、山羊、猪、鱼、蜗牛等食物残渣；柜台壁画绘有拴绳狗
facts.source: 2020年考古发掘新闻稿

facts.content: 传统记为8月24日（小普林尼书信手抄本记'9月朔日前第9日'），2018年炭笔铭文'10月17日'引发争议，2024年《科学进展》综合研究仍支持8月24日
facts.source: 2024年《科学进展》（Science Advances）氩-氩测年研究

[CH01 | 0:00-0:20 | immersive_premise_hook]

I'm in Pompeii. It's August 24th, 79 AD. And in about 32 hours, a mountain is going to bury this entire city — but most of these people will survive. Because they'll run. The ones who stay? Dead in one second.

I'm living in a room about 16 square meters. Three wooden beds. No decorations. And just between you and me, I want to get into those houses on the north side — the ones with 90 rooms and 17-meter-long paintings on the walls.

[CH02 | 0:20-0:36 | authenticity_contract]

Okay, so everything you're seeing comes from public domain sources — Pompeii frescoes, archaeological photographs, and plaster casts. In 1863, archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli figured out he could pour plaster into the hollow spaces left by bodies in the ash and recreate their final moments. What you're looking at is as close as we can get to what was really there.

[CH03 | 0:36-0:56 | mission_briefing]

All right. Here's what I want to do. I need to see the forum — 38 by 142 meters. The amphitheater that holds 20,000 people. At least a few of those 33 bakeries, most of them with their own mills. Some of those 80-plus food bars. Maybe read a couple of the 11,000 graffiti messages scratched into these walls.

And I want to write down what these people are doing in their last ordinary hours. Because I already know how this ends.

[CH04 | 0:56-1:31 | threshold_crossing]

I'm walking north now, away from the workers' quarter near the Stabiana gate, heading toward where the wealthy families live. There's no wall between the neighborhoods. No guards. But the moment I turn onto their streets, I feel it.

A servant glances at me. Another one slows down, looks me over. The doorman at the nearest villa doesn't say a word — he just stands there, blocking the entrance with his body, waiting for me to explain why I'm here.

I'm wearing plain wool. No jewelry. No attendants following me. They can tell. Pompeii didn't need gates to keep people out. Social class was the gate. Where you lived, how you dressed, how many people walked behind you — that told everyone exactly where you belonged. And right now, it's telling them I don't belong here.

But I keep walking.

[CH05 | 1:31-2:46 | daily_life_exploration]

Back in my room now. Let me show you what 16 square meters looks like. Three wooden beds made of rough planks and rope netting. The longest one is about 1.7 meters. I'm going to have to curl up to sleep. The shorter one is maybe 1.4 meters — adjustable, but still short. Under the beds: chamber pots and clay jars. One small window up high. No frescoes. No mosaics. Just bare walls.

In the corner, eight amphora jars and a wooden chest full of horse gear. Okay, so this is actual worker housing. I've stayed in worse Airbnbs.

The smell coming through that window — roasted duck, goat, pork from the food bars down the street. They keep the meat in clay pots built into the counter, and the smoke just hangs in the air all day. It's not bad, honestly. It smells like a city that's alive.

But here's the thing. This city is still healing. In the year 62, seventeen years ago, an earthquake hit — estimated magnitude somewhere between 5.2 and 6.1. It wrecked Pompeii. And they're still rebuilding. I can see scaffolding on half the buildings. The temple of Isis isn't even finished yet.

And the ground is shaking again. Just a little. It's been shaking for days.

[CH06 | 2:46-4:53 | steerage_social_life]

I'm at one of those food bars now — a thermopolium. There's a counter with eight clay jars sunk into it, and a fresco of a dog on a leash painted on the front. The jars have duck, goat, pig, fish, snails. Actual food residue was found in one of these when they excavated it in 2020.

Now, I don't know what was served on this exact day — there's no menu preserved from August 24th, 79 AD. But based on what Roman commoners ate around this time, I'm assuming it's something like bean soup, fish, bread, olive oil, wine.

And since none of the ordinary residents' names were ever recorded — the only person we know by name is Pliny the Elder, the fleet commander — I'm going to imagine what the people next to me might be talking about.

There's a man to my left, maybe mid-thirties, talking about Ostia. He wants to move there, find work at the port. Better money, he says. The woman across from him laughs and says she's saving for her daughter's wedding — two years out, maybe three. Another guy, younger, says he's trying to buy a plot of land outside the city. Just a small one.

They're all talking about later. About next year. About five years from now.

The fish is salty and good. The bread is dense. The wine tastes like vinegar, but I've had worse. This is the best meal I've had in Pompeii. It's also the only meal I've had in Pompeii.

One of them asks if I'm going to the gathering tonight. I say yes.

[CH07 | 4:53-6:17 | communal_celebration]

So, the gathering. It's at the forum tonight, spilling into the amphitheater area. The amphitheater holds 20,000 people. The forum is 38 by 142 meters. It feels like the entire city is here.

Here's some context. Twenty years ago, in the year 59, Pompeii hosted gladiator games. People from the neighboring town of Nuceria came to watch. Pompeii locals and Nuceria locals started yelling at each other. Then it turned into a full brawl. People from Nuceria were seriously hurt — some died. The Senate banned Pompeii from holding public gatherings like this for ten years. That ban just ended. So this? This matters.

Everyone's dancing, drinking, shouting over each other. There's music I don't recognize. Someone hands me wine. A kid runs past me and almost knocks me over. An older woman pulls me into a circle and I have absolutely no idea what I'm doing, but nobody seems to care and I think that's the whole point.

A man about my age, covered in plaster dust — probably a builder — bumps into me and grins. "You're new," he says. I say I'm just visiting. He says, "Well, you're here now. That's what counts."

Later, he pulls me aside. Says, "Come with me for a second."

[CH08 | 6:17-7:40 | confession_and_heist]

All right. Confession. I'm a time traveler from the year 2026 and I'm making a video about Pompeii for people in the future.

He stares at me. I wait. He laughs. Then he stops laughing. "You're serious."

I am.

He says, "What do you need?"

I tell him I need to get into one of those villas on the north side — the big ones with the frescoes and the private baths. He says there's a side door on the north wall of the Villa of the Mysteries. Tonight, during the banquet, the steward steps away for about twenty minutes to eat. That's my window.

I ask him why he's helping me. He shrugs. "If you're telling the truth, this is the strangest thing that's ever happened to me. If you're lying, it's still a good story." He pauses. "Either way, I want to know what you see in there."

We have to go right now. Okay, we need to move. We've got maybe fifteen minutes before someone notices.

At the door, I stop. I say, "Good luck." He says, "With what?" I don't answer. I just say thank you, and then I go.

[CH09 | 7:40-9:00 | forbidden_luxury_reveal]

Oh my god.

This is marble. Actual marble floors. The walls are covered in frescoes — one continuous painting that runs for 17 meters showing some kind of ritual I don't understand. Mystery cult scenes, maybe. The Villa of the Mysteries has about 90 rooms. I'm standing in one of them.

Back in my room, I had 16 square meters, three short beds, and a pot under the bed. This single room is bigger than that. This hallway is bigger than that. And it's all in the same city, on the same day, under the same mountain.

There are people here — wealthy families, their guests — and they're talking quietly, moving through the space like it's normal. Like 90-room houses are normal. I'm trying not to draw attention, but I don't think I belong in rooms like this. I don't think most people in Pompeii belong in rooms like this.

Another villa nearby — the House of the Faun — is even bigger. You could fit a city block inside it. And all of it, everything I just saw in the workers' quarter and everything I'm seeing now, exists in the same 66 hectares.

I need to keep moving before someone asks who I am.

[CH10 | 9:00-9:59 | luxury_catalog]

They're serving a banquet in the largest room. I'm counting at least ten courses, maybe eleven. Whole fish. Roasted meats. Fruit I don't recognize. Wine in silver cups. Nobody in here looks remotely surprised by any of it.

There's a private bath suite — marble basins, heated water, frescoes on the ceiling. A library room with shelves built into the walls. I didn't know private libraries were a thing in Pompeii. I'm learning they were.

I slip outside into the garden. It's dark now. I can see the outline of the mountain against the sky — Vesuvius, black and quiet. From here, it looks peaceful. Beautiful, even. The kind of thing you'd paint.

[CH11 | 9:59-10:36 | dramatic_irony_turn]

Tomorrow is August 24th, 79 AD. That's the date recorded in the manuscripts of Pliny the Younger's letters — "nine days before the Kalends of September." In 2018, a charcoal inscription with the date October 17th sparked some debate, but the most recent research in 2024 still supports August 24th.

I'm not going to tell you the exact time yet, or how fast the ash piled up, or how many people died. I'll count that down for you, hour by hour, when it starts.

But tomorrow is the day. And everyone I met tonight — the man at the food bar who wants to move to Ostia, the woman saving for her daughter's wedding, the builder who helped me get in here — they're all still making plans. Still thinking about next year.

And I'm the only one who knows there isn't going to be a next year. Not for this city.

[CH12 | 10:36-11:35 | plan_rehearsal]

I'm outside the villa now, looking through a window. The banquet is still going. Ten courses, eleven, I lost count. Silver cups catching the lamplight. Laughter. Conversation.

And then the floor shakes. Just a little. A cup shifts on the table. One man glances down, then keeps talking. Nobody stops eating.

Pliny the Younger wrote that earthquakes were so common in Campania that nobody considered them unusual. The ground had been trembling for days — maybe longer — and it was just part of living here. When danger becomes ordinary, you stop calling it danger.

I know what's coming. I know it starts tomorrow around noon. I know the eruption column is going to rise 33 kilometers into the sky. I know ash is going to fall at 15 to 20 centimeters per hour. I know that by the next morning, a pyroclastic surge will hit this city and kill everyone who stayed.

And I can't do anything. I can't walk in there and tell them. Even if I did, who would believe me? A stranger in plain wool talking about a mountain exploding? They'd think I was insane. So I just stand here and watch them eat.

[CH13 | 11:35-12:13 | futile_warning]

I walk back through the streets. Past the forum. Past the food bars, now closed. A merchant is locking up his shop. A mother is calling her children inside. The ground trembles again. One of the kids stops and looks down, curious. His mother tells him to come on, it's just a tremor, they happen all the time.

And that's the problem, isn't it? It happens all the time. So nobody thinks this time is different. Even if I told them, even if I stood in the middle of the forum and shouted, they wouldn't believe me. Because the ground has always shaken. Vesuvius has always been there. And nothing has ever happened before.

So I don't say anything. I just watch them go inside.

The sky is clear. The stars are out. It's a beautiful night.

[CH14 | 12:13-13:12 | countdown_and_impact]

The most recent research, published in 2025, says the eruption lasted about 32 hours. It identified 17 separate pyroclastic flows. The eruption began around noon on August 24th — about an hour earlier than traditionally thought. The pumice phase lasted about 17 hours. The pyroclastic flow phase started the next morning.

August 24th, approximately 12:00 p.m. The eruption begins. Pliny the Younger, watching from 30 kilometers away, describes the column as looking like an umbrella pine tree — a massive trunk with branches spreading at the top, white at first, then streaked with dirt. It rises 33 kilometers into the sky.

1:00 p.m. Pumice stones start to fall. They're light, porous, the size of your fist. People look up. Some of them laugh. Some of them think it's snow. The ground is still shaking, but the ground is always shaking.

Hour by hour, the pumice piles up. 15 to 20 centimeters per hour. By nightfall, it's a meter deep. Roofs start to collapse. Some people leave. Most people stay inside and wait for it to stop. A few people get crushed when their roofs cave in. The eruption is still going.

By the next morning, the pumice is nearly 3 meters deep in some places. And then the pyroclastic flows begin — superheated clouds of gas and ash moving at hundreds of kilometers per hour. The first surge reaches Pompeii sometime that morning. We don't know the exact minute. But we know what it did.

One second. That's how long it took.

[CH15 | 13:12-14:12 | collapse_witnessing]

Okay, here's what we know. Let me lay out the public data and estimates. Pompeii's population is estimated at somewhere between 11,000 and 15,000 people. Herculaneum, the town next door, maybe 5,000. About 1,150 bodies have been found in Pompeii. Another 332 in Herculaneum, including about 300 packed into the boat sheds by the beach — three people per square meter, waiting for rescue by sea. The first pyroclastic surge killed all of them in one second.

Total deaths are estimated at around 2,000, maybe more. Most people escaped. But the ones who stayed? About 38% died during the pumice phase — roofs collapsing, walls falling. About 62% died during the pyroclastic flow phase the next day.

The cause of death is still debated. A 2023 X-ray study supports asphyxiation — victims choked on the ash. But a 2010 study of skeletal remains argued for thermal shock — the surge that hit Pompeii was between 250 and 300 degrees Celsius, hot enough to kill instantly. We're still not entirely sure.

In Herculaneum, they found a man whose brain had been heated to at least 510 degrees Celsius and turned to glass. It's the only known case of vitrified human tissue in an archaeological site. Published in 2025.

I can't watch this anymore. It's just so heartbreaking.

[CH16 | 14:12-15:00 | closure_reflection]

In May 2023, archaeologists found two men who survived the first day. They made it through the pumice phase. They were still alive the next morning. And then an earthquake — one of many during the eruption — brought a wall down on top of them. They were crushed before the pyroclastic flow even arrived. Later excavations found evidence that some survivors and looters returned to the ruins and left graffiti: "House cleared."

There were so many ways to die.

Pliny the Younger, still watching from 30 kilometers away, wrote that the darkness was "not like a moonless or cloudy night, but like a lamp going out in a sealed room." The ash fell like snow, and they had to keep shaking it off so they wouldn't be buried.

For 17 years, Pompeii had been shaking. And people learned to live with it. When danger becomes part of your daily routine, you stop seeing it as danger. You see it as normal. And then one day, normal kills you.

It's one thing to read about Pompeii in a history book. It's another thing to walk these streets, eat at these food bars, meet these people, and know exactly how many hours they have left. You can read about 1,150 bodies. But you can't read what it feels like to stand next to someone who's about to become one of them.

The eruption lasted 32 hours. The warnings lasted 17 years. And nobody saw it coming.

# Optimized Script

[CH01 | 0:00-0:20 | immersive_premise_hook]

I'm in Pompeii. It's August 24th, 79 AD. And in about 32 hours, a mountain is going to bury this entire city — but most of these people will survive. Because they'll run. The ones who stay? Dead in one second.

I'm living in a room about 16 square meters. Three wooden beds. No decorations. Honestly, I'm planning to see those north-side villas — 90 rooms, 17-meter frescoes, the whole thing.

[CH02 | 0:20-0:36 | authenticity_contract]

Everything here comes from real sources — frescoes, photos, plaster casts. In 1863, archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli figured out he could pour plaster into the hollow spaces left by bodies in the ash. This is the closest reconstruction possible from what survived.

[CH03 | 0:36-0:56 | mission_briefing]

I need to see the forum, the amphitheater, the bakeries, the food bars. And I want to record what people are doing in their last normal hours. Because I know what's coming.

[CH04 | 0:56-1:31 | threshold_crossing]

I'm walking north now, away from the workers' quarter near the Stabiana gate, heading toward where the wealthy families live. There's no wall between the neighborhoods. No guards. But the moment I turn onto their streets, I feel it.

A servant glances at me. Another one slows down, looks me over. The doorman at the nearest villa doesn't say a word — he just stands there, blocking the entrance with his body, waiting for me to explain why I'm here.

I'm wearing plain wool. No jewelry. No attendants following me. They can tell. Social class was the gate. And right now, it's telling them I don't belong here.

But I keep walking.

[CH05 | 1:31-2:46 | daily_life_exploration]

Back in my room now. Let me show you what 16 square meters looks like. Three wooden beds made of rough planks and rope netting. The longest one is about 1.7 meters. I'm going to have to curl up to sleep. Under the beds: chamber pots and clay jars. One small window up high. No frescoes. No mosaics. Just bare walls.

In the corner, eight amphora jars and a wooden chest full of horse gear. This is actual worker housing.

The smell coming through that window — roasted duck, goat, pork from the food bars down the street. They keep the meat in clay pots built into the counter, and the smoke just hangs in the air all day.

But here's the thing. This city is still healing. In the year 62, on February 5th, an earthquake hit — estimated magnitude 5.2 to 6.1. It wrecked Pompeii. And they're still rebuilding. I can see scaffolding on half the buildings. The temple of Isis isn't even finished yet.

And the ground is shaking again. Just a little. It's been shaking for days.

[CH06 | 2:46-4:53 | steerage_social_life]

I'm at one of those food bars now — a thermopolium. There's a counter with eight clay jars sunk into it, and a fresco of a dog on a leash painted on the front. The jars have duck, goat, pig, fish, snails. Actual food residue was found in one of these when they excavated it in 2020.

Now, I don't know what was served on this exact day — there's no menu preserved from August 24th, 79 AD. But based on what Roman commoners ate in this period, I'm assuming it's something like bean soup, fish, bread, olive oil, wine.

And since none of the ordinary residents' names were ever recorded — the only victim we can confirm by name is Pliny the Elder, the fleet commander — I'm going to imagine what the people next to me might be talking about.

There's a man to my left, maybe mid-thirties, talking about Ostia. He wants to move there, find work at the port. Better money, he says. The woman across from him laughs and says she's saving for her daughter's wedding — two years out, maybe three. Another guy, younger, says he's trying to buy a plot of land outside the city. Just a small one.

They're all talking about later. About next year. About five years from now.

The fish is salty and good. The bread is dense. The wine tastes like vinegar, but I've had worse. This is the best meal I've had in Pompeii. It's also the only meal I've had in Pompeii.

One of them asks if I'm going to the gathering tonight. I say yes.

[CH07 | 4:53-6:17 | communal_celebration]

So, the gathering. It's at the forum tonight, spilling into the amphitheater area. The amphitheater holds 20,000 people. The forum is 38 by 142 meters. It feels like the entire city is here.

Here's some context. Twenty years ago, in the year 59, Pompeii hosted gladiator games. People from the neighboring town of Nuceria came to watch. Pompeii locals and Nuceria locals started yelling at each other. Then it turned into a full brawl. People from Nuceria were seriously hurt — some died. The Senate banned Pompeii from holding public gatherings like this for ten years. That ban just ended. So this matters.

Everyone's dancing, drinking, shouting over each other. There's music I don't recognize. Someone hands me wine. A kid runs past me and almost knocks me over. An older woman pulls me into a circle and I'm clearly terrible at this, but no one minds — that's what makes it feel right.

A man about my age, covered in plaster dust — probably a builder — bumps into me and grins. "You're new," he says. I say I'm just visiting. He says, "Well, you're here now. That's what counts."

Later, he pulls me aside. Says, "Come with me for a second."

[CH08 | 6:17-7:40 | confession_and_heist]

Okay, full truth: I'm from 2026. This is a video. You're in it. And tomorrow, everything changes.

He stares at me. I wait. He laughs. Then he stops laughing. "You're serious."

I am.

He says, "What do you need?"

I tell him I need to get into one of those villas on the north side — the big ones with the frescoes and the private baths. He says there's a side door on the north wall of the Villa of the Mysteries. Tonight, during the banquet, the steward steps away for about twenty minutes to eat. That's my window.

I ask him why he's helping me. He shrugs. "If you're telling the truth, this is the strangest thing that's ever happened to me. If you're lying, it's still a good story." He pauses. "Either way, I want to know what you see in there."

We need to leave. Now. Maybe fifteen minutes before someone spots us.

At the door, I stop. I say, "Good luck." He says, "With what?" I don't answer. I just say thank you, and then I go.

[CH09 | 7:40-9:00 | forbidden_luxury_reveal]

Oh my god.

This is marble. Actual marble floors. The walls are covered in frescoes — one continuous painting that runs for 17 meters showing some kind of ritual I don't understand. Mystery cult scenes, maybe. The Villa of the Mysteries has about 90 rooms. I'm standing in one of them.

Back in my room, I had 16 square meters, three short beds, and a pot under the bed. This single room is bigger than that. This hallway is bigger than that. And it's all in the same city, on the same day, under the same mountain.

There are people here — wealthy families, their guests — and they're talking quietly, moving through the space like it's normal. Like 90-room houses are normal. No one here finds this unusual. It's just another dinner.

Another villa nearby — the House of the Faun — is even bigger. You could fit a city block inside it. And all of it, everything I just saw in the workers' quarter and everything I'm seeing now, exists in the same 66 hectares.

I need to keep moving before someone asks who I am.

[CH10 | 9:00-9:59 | luxury_catalog]

They're serving a banquet in the largest room. I'm counting at least ten courses, maybe eleven. Whole fish. Roasted meats. Fruit I don't recognize. Wine in silver cups.

There's a private bath suite — marble basins, heated water, frescoes on the ceiling. A library room with shelves built into the walls. I didn't know private libraries were a thing in Pompeii. I'm learning they were.

I slip outside into the garden. It's dark now. I can see the outline of the mountain against the sky — Vesuvius, black and quiet. From here, it looks peaceful. Beautiful, even. The kind of thing you'd paint.

[CH11 | 9:59-10:36 | dramatic_irony_turn]

Tomorrow is August 24th, 79 AD. That's the date recorded in Pliny the Younger's letters. A 2018 inscription sparked some debate, but the most recent research in 2024 still supports August 24th.

I'm not going to tell you the exact time yet, or how fast the ash piled up, or how many people died. I'll count that down for you, hour by hour, when it starts.

But tomorrow is the day. And the man at the food bar who wants to move to Ostia, the woman saving for her daughter's wedding, the builder who helped me get in here — they're all still making plans.

And I'm the only one who knows there isn't going to be a next year. Not for this city.

[CH12 | 10:36-11:35 | plan_rehearsal]

I'm outside the villa now, looking through a window. The banquet is still going. Ten courses, eleven, I lost count. Silver cups catching the lamplight. Laughter. Conversation.

And then the floor shakes. Just a little. A cup shifts on the table. One man glances down, then keeps talking. Nobody stops eating.

Pliny the Younger wrote that earthquakes were so common in Campania that nobody considered them unusual. The ground had been trembling for days — maybe longer — and it was just part of living here. When danger becomes ordinary, you stop calling it danger.

And I can't do anything. I can't walk in there and tell them. Even if I did, who would believe me? A stranger in plain wool talking about a mountain exploding? They'd think I was insane. So I just stand here and watch them eat.

[CH13 | 11:35-12:13 | futile_warning]

I walk back through the streets. Past the forum. Past the food bars, now closed. A merchant is locking up his shop. A mother is calling her children inside. The ground trembles again. One of the kids stops and looks down, curious. His mother tells him to come on, it's just a tremor, they happen all the time.

That's the problem. It happens all the time. Nobody thinks this time is different.

So I don't say anything. I just watch them go inside.

The sky is clear. The stars are out. It's a beautiful night.

[CH14 | 12:13-13:12 | countdown_and_impact]

August 24th, approximately 12:00 p.m. The eruption begins. Pliny the Younger, watching from 30 kilometers away, describes the column as looking like an umbrella pine tree — a massive trunk with branches spreading at the top. It rises 33 kilometers into the sky.

1:00 p.m. Pumice stones start to fall. They're light, porous, the size of your fist. People look up. Some of them laugh. Some of them think it's snow.

Hour by hour, the pumice piles up. 15 to 20 centimeters per hour. By nightfall, it's over a meter deep. Roofs start to collapse. Some people leave. Most people stay inside and wait for it to stop. A few people get crushed when their roofs cave in.

By the next morning, the pumice is nearly 3 meters deep — in some places, more. And then the pyroclastic flows begin — superheated clouds of gas and ash moving at hundreds of kilometers per hour. The first surge reaches Pompeii sometime that morning.

One second. That's how long it took.

Some people survived the first day. They made it through the pumice phase. And then an earthquake brought a wall down on top of them.

[CH15 | 13:12-14:12 | collapse_witnessing]

About 1,150 bodies in Pompeii, 332 in Herculaneum — over 1,500 found so far. But the estimated death toll is around 2,000, maybe more. Most people escaped.

Of the bodies found in Pompeii, about 38% died during the pumice phase — roofs collapsing, walls falling. About 62% during the pyroclastic surge.

The cause of death is still debated. A 2023 X-ray study supports asphyxiation. But a 2010 study argued for thermal shock — the surge was between 250 and 300 degrees Celsius, hot enough to kill instantly.

In Herculaneum, about 300 people packed into the boat sheds by the beach — three people per square meter, waiting for rescue by sea. The first surge killed all of them in one second.

They found a man whose brain had been heated to at least 510 degrees Celsius and turned to glass. It's the only known case of vitrified human tissue in an archaeological site.

I can't watch this anymore. It's just so heartbreaking.

[CH16 | 14:12-15:00 | closure_reflection]

In May 2023, archaeologists found two men who survived the first day. They were still alive the next morning. And then an earthquake brought a wall down on top of them. They were crushed before the pyroclastic flow even arrived.

There were so many ways to die.

Pliny the Younger wrote that the darkness was "not like a moonless or cloudy night, but like a lamp going out in a sealed room." The ash fell like snow, and they had to keep shaking it off so they wouldn't be buried.

For 17 years since the earthquake of 62, Pompeii had been shaking. Pliny wrote that earthquakes were so common in Campania, nobody thought twice about them. When danger becomes part of your daily routine, you stop seeing it as danger. You see it as normal. And then one day, normal kills you.

You can read about 1,150 bodies in a book. Standing next to someone who's about to become one — that's different.

The eruption lasted 32 hours. The warnings lasted 17 years. And nobody saw it coming.

---

final_script:
# Optimized Script

[CH01 | 0:00-0:20 | immersive_premise_hook]

I'm in Pompeii. It's August 24th, 79 AD. And in just over a day, a mountain is going to bury this entire city — but most of these people will survive. Because they'll run. The ones who stay? Most of them won't make it past the second day.

I'm in the workers' quarter. And I'm planning to see those villas on the north side — 90 rooms, 17-meter frescoes, the whole thing.

[CH02 | 0:20-0:36 | authenticity_contract]

Everything here comes from real sources — frescoes, photos, plaster casts. In 1863, archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli figured out he could pour plaster into the hollow spaces left by bodies in the ash. The date is traditionally recorded as August 24th, and recent studies still support that. This is the closest reconstruction possible from what survived.

[CH03 | 0:36-0:56 | mission_briefing]

I need to see the forum, the amphitheater, the bakeries, the food bars. And I want to record what people are doing in their last normal hours. Because I know what's coming.

[CH04 | 0:56-1:31 | threshold_crossing]

I'm walking north now, away from the workers' quarter near the Stabiana gate, heading toward where the wealthy families live. There's no wall between the neighborhoods. No guards. But the moment I turn onto their streets, I feel it.

I'm wearing plain wool. Dark brown — the cheapest dye. Theirs is purple-trimmed. A servant glances at my hands. No rings. Another looks past me, checking for attendants. There are none. The doorman at the nearest villa doesn't say a word — he just stands there, blocking the entrance with his body, waiting for me to explain why I'm here.

I'm wearing plain wool. No jewelry. No attendants. Social class was the gate. And right now, it's locked.

But I keep walking.

[CH05 | 1:31-2:46 | daily_life_exploration]

Back in my room now. Let me show you what 16 square meters looks like. Three wooden beds made of rough planks and rope netting. The longest one is about 1.7 meters. I'm going to have to curl up to sleep. Under the beds: chamber pots and clay jars. One small window up high. No frescoes. No mosaics. Just bare walls.

In the corner, eight amphora jars and a wooden chest full of horse gear. This is actual worker housing.

The smell coming through that window — roasted duck, goat, pork from the food bars down the street. They keep the meat in clay pots built into the counter, and the smoke just hangs in the air all day.

But here's the thing. This city is still healing. In 62 AD, on February 5th, a major earthquake hit. It wrecked Pompeii. And they're still rebuilding. I can see scaffolding on half the buildings. The temple of Isis isn't even finished yet.

And the ground is shaking again. Just a little. It's been shaking for days.

[CH06 | 2:46-4:53 | steerage_social_life]

I'm at one of those food bars now — a thermopolium. There's a counter with eight clay jars sunk into it, and a fresco of a dog on a leash painted on the front. The jars have duck, goat, pig, fish, snails. Actual food residue was found in one of these when they excavated it in 2020.

Now, I don't know what was served on this exact day — there's no menu preserved from August 24th, 79 AD. But based on what Roman commoners ate in this period, I'm assuming it's something like bean soup, fish, bread, olive oil, wine.

And since none of the ordinary residents' names were ever recorded — the only victim we can confirm by name is Pliny the Elder, the fleet commander — I'm going to imagine what the people next to me might be talking about.

There's a man to my left, maybe mid-thirties, talking about Ostia. He wants to move there, find work at the port. Better money, he says. There's a woman across from me, maybe forty, hands rough from years of spinning wool. She laughs when she talks about her daughter — 'She says unless there's music at the wedding, she won't marry. So I'm saving. Two years, maybe three. Just enough to hire a lyre player.' She pauses. 'She's picky. But she's worth it.' Another guy, younger, says he's trying to buy a plot of land outside the city. Just a small one.

They're all talking about later. About next year. About five years from now.

The fish is salty and good. The bread is dense. The wine tastes like vinegar, but I've had worse. This is the best meal I've had in Pompeii. It's also the only meal I've had in Pompeii.

One of them asks if I'm going to the gathering tonight. I say yes.

[CH07 | 4:53-6:17 | communal_celebration]

So, the gathering. It's at the forum tonight, spilling into the amphitheater area. The amphitheater holds about 20,000 people. The forum is 38 by 142 meters. It feels like the entire city is here.

Here's some context. Twenty years ago, in the year 59, Pompeii hosted gladiator games. People from the neighboring town of Nuceria came to watch. Pompeii locals and Nuceria locals started yelling at each other. Then it turned into a full brawl. People from Nuceria were seriously hurt — some died. The Senate banned Pompeii from holding public gatherings like this for ten years. That ban just ended. So this matters.

Everyone's dancing, drinking, shouting over each other. There's music I don't recognize. Someone hands me wine. A kid runs past me and almost knocks me over. An older woman pulls me into a circle and I'm clearly terrible at this, but no one minds — that's what makes it feel right.

A man about my age, covered in plaster dust — probably a builder — bumps into me and grins. "You're new," he says. I say I'm just visiting. He pulls me into the circle, tries to teach me a step. I step on his foot. He laughs. "Don't worry. This dance is supposed to be messy. That's the whole point."

Later, he pulls me aside. Says, "Come with me for a second."

[CH08 | 6:17-7:40 | confession_and_heist]

Okay, full truth: I'm from 2026. This is a video. You're in it. And tomorrow, everything changes.

He stares at me. I wait. He laughs. Then he stops laughing. "You're serious."

I am.

He says, "What do you need?"

I tell him I need to get into one of those villas on the north side — the big ones with the frescoes and the private baths. He says there's a side door on the north wall of the Villa of the Mysteries. The banquet just started. He usually goes to the kitchen during the third course. We have maybe fifteen minutes.

I ask him why he's helping me. He shrugs. "If you're telling the truth, this is the strangest thing that's ever happened to me. If you're lying, it's still a good story." He pauses. "Either way, I want to know what you see in there."

We need to leave. Now. Maybe fifteen minutes before someone spots us.

At the door, I stop. I say thank you. He nods, then looks at me for a long moment, like he's trying to remember my face. "Good luck," he says. "With whatever you're really here for."

[CH09 | 7:40-9:00 | forbidden_luxury_reveal]

Oh my god.

This is marble. Actual marble floors. The walls are covered in frescoes — one continuous painting that runs for 17 meters. A woman kneeling. A winged figure behind her, holding a whip. This isn't decoration. This is belief. And I just walked into someone's sacred space. The Villa of the Mysteries has about 90 rooms. I'm standing in one of them.

Back in my room, I had 16 square meters, three short beds, and a pot under the bed. This single room is bigger than that. This hallway is bigger than that. And it's all in the same city, on the same day, under the same mountain.

There are people here — wealthy families, their guests — and they're talking quietly, moving through the space like it's normal. Like 90-room houses are normal. No one here finds this unusual. It's just another dinner.

Another villa nearby — the House of the Faun — is even bigger. You could fit a city block inside it. And all of it, everything I just saw in the workers' quarter and everything I'm seeing now, exists in the same 66 hectares.

I need to keep moving before someone asks who I am.

[CH10 | 9:00-9:59 | luxury_catalog]

versions.text:
# Optimized Script

[CH01 | 0:00-0:20 | immersive_premise_hook]

I'm in Pompeii. It's August 24th, 79 AD. And in about 32 hours, a mountain is going to bury this entire city — but most of these people will survive. Because they'll run. The ones who stay? Dead in one second.

I'm living in a room about 16 square meters. Three wooden beds. No decorations. Honestly, I'm planning to see those north-side villas — 90 rooms, 17-meter frescoes, the whole thing.

[CH02 | 0:20-0:36 | authenticity_contract]

Everything here comes from real sources — frescoes, photos, plaster casts. In 1863, archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli figured out he could pour plaster into the hollow spaces left by bodies in the ash. This is the closest reconstruction possible from what survived.

[CH03 | 0:36-0:56 | mission_briefing]

I need to see the forum, the amphitheater, the bakeries, the food bars. And I want to record what people are doing in their last normal hours. Because I know what's coming.

[CH04 | 0:56-1:31 | threshold_crossing]

I'm walking north now, away from the workers' quarter near the Stabiana gate, heading toward where the wealthy families live. There's no wall between the neighborhoods. No guards. But the moment I turn onto their streets, I feel it.

A servant glances at me. Another one slows down, looks me over. The doorman at the nearest villa doesn't say a word — he just stands there, blocking the entrance with his body, waiting for me to explain why I'm here.

I'm wearing plain wool. No jewelry. No attendants following me. They can tell. Social class was the gate. And right now, it's telling them I don't belong here.

But I keep walking.

[CH05 | 1:31-2:46 | daily_life_exploration]

Back in my room now. Let me show you what 16 square meters looks like. Three wooden beds made of rough planks and rope netting. The longest one is about 1.7 meters. I'm going to have to curl up to sleep. Under the beds: chamber pots and clay jars. One small window up high. No frescoes. No mosaics. Just bare walls.

In the corner, eight amphora jars and a wooden chest full of horse gear. This is actual worker housing.

The smell coming through that window — roasted duck, goat, pork from the food bars down the street. They keep the meat in clay pots built into the counter, and the smoke just hangs in the air all day.

But here's the thing. This city is still healing. In the year 62, on February 5th, an earthquake hit — estimated magnitude 5.2 to 6.1. It wrecked Pompeii. And they're still rebuilding. I can see scaffolding on half the buildings. The temple of Isis isn't even finished yet.

And the ground is shaking again. Just a little. It's been shaking for days.

[CH06 | 2:46-4:53 | steerage_social_life]

I'm at one of those food bars now — a thermopolium. There's a counter with eight clay jars sunk into it, and a fresco of a dog on a leash painted on the front. The jars have duck, goat, pig, fish, snails. Actual food residue was found in one of these when they excavated it in 2020.

Now, I don't know what was served on this exact day — there's no menu preserved from August 24th, 79 AD. But based on what Roman commoners ate in this period, I'm assuming it's something like bean soup, fish, bread, olive oil, wine.

And since none of the ordinary residents' names were ever recorded — the only victim we can confirm by name is Pliny the Elder, the fleet commander — I'm going to imagine what the people next to me might be talking about.

There's a man to my left, maybe mid-thirties, talking about Ostia. He wants to move there, find work at the port. Better money, he says. The woman across from him laughs and says she's saving for her daughter's wedding — two years out, maybe three. Another guy, younger, says he's trying to buy a plot of land outside the city. Just a small one.

They're all talking about later. About next year. About five years from now.

The fish is salty and good. The bread is dense. The wine tastes like vinegar, but I've had worse. This is the best meal I've had in Pompeii. It's also the only meal I've had in Pompeii.

One of them asks if I'm going to the gathering tonight. I say yes.

[CH07 | 4:53-6:17 | communal_celebration]

So, the gathering. It's at the forum tonight, spilling into the amphitheater area. The amphitheater holds 20,000 people. The forum is 38 by 142 meters. It feels like the entire city is here.

Here's some context. Twenty years ago, in the year 59, Pompeii hosted gladiator games. People from the neighboring town of Nuceria came to watch. Pompeii locals and Nuceria locals started yelling at each other. Then it turned into a full brawl. People from Nuceria were seriously hurt — some died. The Senate banned Pompeii from holding public gatherings like this for ten years. That ban just ended. So this matters.

Everyone's dancing, drinking, shouting over each other. There's music I don't recognize. Someone hands me wine. A kid runs past me and almost knocks me over. An older woman pulls me into a circle and I'm clearly terrible at this, but no one minds — that's what makes it feel right.

A man about my age, covered in plaster dust — probably a builder — bumps into me and grins. "You're new," he says. I say I'm just visiting. He says, "Well, you're here now. That's what counts."

Later, he pulls me aside. Says, "Come with me for a second."

[CH08 | 6:17-7:40 | confession_and_heist]

Okay, full truth: I'm from 2026. This is a video. You're in it. And tomorrow, everything changes.

He stares at me. I wait. He laughs. Then he stops laughing. "You're serious."

I am.

He says, "What do you need?"

I tell him I need to get into one of those villas on the north side — the big ones with the frescoes and the private baths. He says there's a side door on the north wall of the Villa of the Mysteries. Tonight, during the banquet, the steward steps away for about twenty minutes to eat. That's my window.

I ask him why he's helping me. He shrugs. "If you're telling the truth, this is the strangest thing that's ever happened to me. If you're lying, it's still a good story." He pauses. "Either way, I want to know what you see in there."

We need to leave. Now. Maybe fifteen minutes before someone spots us.

At the door, I stop. I say, "Good luck." He says, "With what?" I don't answer. I just say thank you, and then I go.

[CH09 | 7:40-9:00 | forbidden_luxury_reveal]

Oh my god.

This is marble. Actual marble floors. The walls are covered in frescoes — one continuous painting that runs for 17 meters showing some kind of ritual I don't understand. Mystery cult scenes, maybe. The Villa of the Mysteries has about 90 rooms. I'm standing in one of them.

Back in my room, I had 16 square meters, three short beds, and a pot under the bed. This single room is bigger than that. This hallway is bigger than that. And it's all in the same city, on the same day, under the same mountain.

There are people here — wealthy families, their guests — and they're talking quietly, moving through the space like it's normal. Like 90-room houses are normal. No one here finds this unusual. It's just another dinner.

Another villa nearby — the House of the Faun — is even bigger. You could fit a city block inside it. And all of it, everything I just saw in the workers' quarter and everything I'm seeing now, exists in the same 66 hectares.

I need to keep moving before someone asks who I am.

[CH10 | 9:00-9:59 | luxury_catalog]

They're serving a banquet in the largest room. I'm counting at least ten courses, maybe eleven. Whole fish. Roasted meats. Fruit I don't recognize. Wine in silver cups.

There's a private bath suite — marble basins, heated water, frescoes on the ceiling. A library room with shelves built into the walls. I didn't know private libraries were a thing in Pompeii. I'm learning they were.

I slip outside into the garden. It's dark now. I can see the outline of the mountain against the sky — Vesuvius, black and quiet. From here, it looks peaceful. Beautiful, even. The kind of thing you'd paint.

[CH11 | 9:59-10:36 | dramatic_irony_turn]

Tomorrow is August 24th, 79 AD. That's the date recorded in Pliny the Younger's letters. A 2018 inscription sparked some debate, but the most recent research in 2024 still supports August 24th.

I'm not going to tell you the exact time yet, or how fast the ash piled up, or how many people died. I'll count that down for you, hour by hour, when it starts.

But tomorrow is the day. And the man at the food bar who wants to move to Ostia, the woman saving for her daughter's wedding, the builder who helped me get in here — they're all still making plans.

And I'm the only one who knows there isn't going to be a next year. Not for this city.

[CH12 | 10:36-11:35 | plan_rehearsal]

I'm outside the villa now, looking through a window. The banquet is still going. Ten courses, eleven, I lost count. Silver cups catching the lamplight. Laughter. Conversation.

And then the floor shakes. Just a little. A cup shifts on the table. One man glances down, then keeps talking. Nobody stops eating.

Pliny the Younger wrote that earthquakes were so common in Campania that nobody considered them unusual. The ground had been trembling for days — maybe longer — and it was just part of living here. When danger becomes ordinary, you stop calling it danger.

And I can't do anything. I can't walk in there and tell them. Even if I did, who would believe me? A stranger in plain wool talking about a mountain exploding? They'd think I was insane. So I just stand here and watch them eat.

[CH13 | 11:35-12:13 | futile_warning]

I walk back through the streets. Past the forum. Past the food bars, now closed. A merchant is locking up his shop. A mother is calling her children inside. The ground trembles again. One of the kids stops and looks down, curious. His mother tells him to come on, it's just a tremor, they happen all the time.

That's the problem. It happens all the time. Nobody thinks this time is different.

So I don't say anything. I just watch them go inside.

The sky is clear. The stars are out. It's a beautiful night.

[CH14 | 12:13-13:12 | countdown_and_impact]

August 24th, approximately 12:00 p.m. The eruption begins. Pliny the Younger, watching from 30 kilometers away, describes the column as looking like an umbrella pine tree — a massive trunk with branches spreading at the top. It rises 33 kilometers into the sky.

1:00 p.m. Pumice stones start to fall. They're light, porous, the size of your fist. People look up. Some of them laugh. Some of them think it's snow.

Hour by hour, the pumice piles up. 15 to 20 centimeters per hour. By nightfall, it's over a meter deep. Roofs start to collapse. Some people leave. Most people stay inside and wait for it to stop. A few people get crushed when their roofs cave in.

By the next morning, the pumice is 2.8 to 3 meters deep. And then the pyroclastic flows begin — superheated clouds of gas and ash moving at hundreds of kilometers per hour. The first surge reaches Pompeii sometime that morning.

One second. That's how long it took.

Some people survived the first day. They made it through the pumice phase. And then an earthquake brought a wall down on top of them.

[CH15 | 13:12-14:12 | collapse_witnessing]

About 1,150 bodies in Pompeii, 332 in Herculaneum — over 1,500 found so far. But the estimated death toll is around 2,000, maybe more. Most people escaped.

Of the bodies found in Pompeii, about 38% died during the pumice phase — roofs collapsing, walls falling. About 62% during the pyroclastic surge.

The cause of death is still debated. A 2023 X-ray study supports asphyxiation. But a 2010 study argued for thermal shock — the surge was between 250 and 300 degrees Celsius, hot enough to kill instantly.

In Herculaneum, about 300 people packed into the boat sheds by the beach — three people per square meter, waiting for rescue by sea. The first surge killed all of them in one second.

In Herculaneum, they found a man whose brain had been heated to at least 510 degrees Celsius and turned to glass. It's the only known case of vitrified human tissue in an archaeological site.

I can't watch this anymore. It's just so heartbreaking.

[CH16 | 14:12-15:00 | closure_reflection]

In May 2023, archaeologists found two men who survived the first day. They were still alive the next morning. And then an earthquake brought a wall down on top of them. They were crushed before the pyroclastic flow even arrived.

There were so many ways to die.

Pliny the Younger wrote that the darkness was "not like a moonless or cloudy night, but like a lamp going out in a sealed room." The ash fell like snow, and they had to keep shaking it off so they wouldn't be buried.

For 17 years since the earthquake of 62, Pompeii had been shaking. Pliny wrote that earthquakes were so common in Campania, nobody thought twice about them. When danger becomes part of your daily routine, you stop seeing it as danger. You see it as normal. And then one day, normal kills you.

You can read about 1,150 bodies in a book. Standing next to someone who's about to become one — that's different.

The eruption lasted 32 hours. The warnings lasted 17 years. And nobody saw it coming.

I slip outside into the garden. It's dark now. I can see the outline of the mountain against the sky — Vesuvius, black and quiet. From here, it looks peaceful. Beautiful, even. The kind of thing you'd paint.

[CH11 | 9:59-10:36 | dramatic_irony_turn]

Tomorrow is August 24th, 79 AD. Traditionally recorded as August 24th — a 2018 inscription raised questions, but most scholars still use this date.

I'm not going to tell you the exact time yet, or how fast the ash piled up, or how many people died. I'll count that down for you, hour by hour, when it starts.

But tomorrow is the day. And the man at the food bar who wants to move to Ostia, the woman saving for her daughter's wedding, the builder who helped me get in here — they're all still making plans.

And I'm the only one who knows there isn't going to be a next year. Not for this city.

[CH12 | 10:36-11:35 | plan_rehearsal]

I'm outside the villa now, looking through a window. The banquet is still going. Ten courses, eleven, I lost count. Silver cups catching the lamplight. Laughter. Conversation.

And then the floor shakes. Just a little. A cup shifts on the table. One man glances down, then keeps talking. Nobody stops eating.

Pliny the Younger wrote that earthquakes were so common in Campania that nobody considered them unusual. The ground had been trembling for days — maybe longer — and it was just part of living here. When danger becomes ordinary, you stop calling it danger.

And I can't do anything. I can't walk in there and tell them. Even if I did, who would believe me? A stranger in plain wool talking about a mountain exploding? They'd think I was insane. So I just stand here and watch them eat.

[CH13 | 11:35-12:13 | futile_warning]

I walk back through the streets. Past the forum. Past the food bars, now closed. A merchant is locking up his shop. A mother is calling her children inside. The ground trembles again. One of the kids stops and looks down, curious. His mother tells him to come on, it's just a tremor, they happen all the time.

That's the problem. It happens all the time. Nobody thinks this time is different.

So I don't say anything. I just watch them go inside.

The sky is clear. The stars are out. It's a beautiful night.

[CH14 | 12:13-13:12 | countdown_and_impact]

August 24th, around noon. The eruption begins. Pliny the Younger describes the column as looking like an umbrella pine tree — a massive trunk with branches spreading at the top. It rises 33 kilometers into the sky.

1:00 p.m. Pumice stones start to fall. Light, porous, the size of your fist. People look up. Some laugh. Some think it's snow.

Hour by hour, the pumice piles up. 15 to 20 centimeters per hour. By nightfall, over a meter deep. Roofs start to collapse. Some people leave. Most stay inside and wait. A few get crushed when their roofs cave in.

By the next morning, the pumice is 2.8 to 3 meters deep. And then the pyroclastic flows begin — superheated clouds of gas and ash moving at hundreds of kilometers per hour.

Some people survived the first day. They made it through the pumice phase. And then an earthquake brought a wall down on top of them.

[CH15 | 13:12-14:12 | collapse_witnessing]

About 1,150 bodies in Pompeii, 332 in Herculaneum — over 1,500 found so far. But the estimated death toll is around 2,000, maybe more. Most people escaped.

Of the bodies found in Pompeii, about 38% died during the pumice phase — roofs collapsing, walls falling. About 62% during the pyroclastic surge.

The cause of death is still debated. A 2023 X-ray study supports asphyxiation. But a 2010 study argued for thermal shock — the surge was between 250 and 300 degrees Celsius, hot enough to kill instantly.

In Herculaneum, about 300 people packed into the boat sheds by the beach, waiting for rescue by sea. The first surge killed all of them.

In Herculaneum, they found a man whose brain had been heated to at least 510 degrees Celsius and turned to glass. It's the only known case of vitrified human tissue in an archaeological site.

I can't watch this anymore.

[CH16 | 14:12-15:00 | closure_reflection]

In May 2023, archaeologists found two men who survived the first day. They were still alive the next morning. And then an earthquake brought a wall down on top of them.

Pliny the Younger wrote that the darkness was "not like a moonless or cloudy night, but like a lamp going out in a sealed room." The ash fell like snow, and they had to keep shaking it off so they wouldn't be buried.

For 17 years since the earthquake of 62, Pompeii had been shaking. Pliny wrote that earthquakes were so common in Campania, nobody thought twice about them.

You can read about 1,150 bodies in a book. Standing next to someone who's about to become one — that's different.

When danger becomes part of your daily routine, you stop seeing it as danger — until the countdown runs out.
